question.prompt: Six chairs are arranged around a round table. Two students and two teachers randomly select four of the chairs to sit in. What is the probability that the two students will sit in two adjacent chairs and the two teachers will also sit in two adjacent chairs?

solutions.title: Seat the students first
solutions.explanation:
Seat the students first. Once they occupy adjacent chairs, the remaining four chairs form one consecutive block, making the teachers' possibilities easy to count.

After the first student sits, the second student has \(5\) equally likely chair choices. Exactly \(2\) are beside the first student, so
\[
P(\text{students adjacent})=\frac25.
\]
Given that the students are adjacent, call the remaining chairs \(A,B,C,D\) in order around the table. The teachers can occupy any of
\[
\binom42=\frac{4\cdot3}{2}=6
\]
pairs. These pairs are equally likely because each allows two orders for the teachers. Exactly three pairs, \(AB\), \(BC\), and \(CD\), are adjacent. Thus
\[
P(\text{teachers adjacent}\mid\text{students adjacent})=\frac36.
\]
Multiplying the first probability by this conditional probability gives
\[
P(\text{both pairs adjacent})=\frac25\cdot\frac36=\boxed{\frac15}.
\]
The answer is \(\text{(B)}\).
